plain_english: Among the time-wasters, I put drunks and party animals at the top of the list. No one wastes time more shamefully than they do. At least other people — even if they chase fake glory — deserve some credit for trying. You can name all the misers, the angry people, the ones who hate and fight for no reason. Sure, they're all sinning. But at least they sin like human beings. The sin of gluttons and perverts is just disgusting. Look at how these people spend their hours. Count up the time they spend scheming, plotting, being afraid, giving fake compliments, making promises for themselves and others, throwing banquets that become serious business ventures. You'll see that their pleasures and pains give them no rest at all.
original_excerpt: Among these I reckon in the first place those who devote their time to nothing but drinking and debauchery: for no men are busied more shamefully: the others, although the glory which they pursue is but a counterfeit, still deserve some credit for their pursuit of it—though you may tell me of misers, of passionate men, of men who hate and who even wage war without a cause—yet all such men sin like men: but the sin of those who are given up to gluttony and lust is a disgraceful one. Examine all the hours of their lives: consider how much time they spend in calculation, how much in plotting, how much in fear, how much in giving and deceiving flattery, how much in entering into recognizances for themselves or for others, how much in banquets, which indeed become a serious business, you will see that they are not allowed any breathing time either by their pleasures or their pains.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: Everyone agrees on this: you can't do anything well — whether it's speaking or writing — if your mind is busy with something else. Nothing takes root in a mind that's pulled in different directions and pushes away whatever you try to put into it. No one knows less about living than someone obsessed with business. There's nothing harder to learn than how to live. Other skills have plenty of teachers everywhere. Some can be learned so well by children that they can teach them to others. But learning how to live takes your entire lifetime. And here's what might surprise you even more: learning how to die takes your entire lifetime too.
original_excerpt: Finally, all are agreed that nothing, neither eloquence nor literature, can be done properly by one who is occupied with something else; for nothing can take deep root in a mind which is directed to some other subject, and which rejects whatever you try to stuff into it. No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge. Other arts have many folk everywhere who profess to teach them: some of them can be so thoroughly learned by mere boys, that they are able to teach them to others: but one's whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one's whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: Many great people have given up everything that held them back. They abandoned wealth, work, and pleasure to spend their whole lives learning how to live well. Yet most of them die admitting they still don't know how to live — let alone how to live wisely. Trust me, it takes an extraordinary person to protect their time from being stolen. Someone who rises above ordinary human weaknesses. That's why such a person's life feels very long. They dedicate every moment to themselves. No time sits wasted or neglected or under someone else's control. They find nothing valuable enough to trade for their time, which they guard fiercely.
original_excerpt: Many excellent men have freed themselves from all hindrances, have given up riches, business, and pleasure, and have made it their duty to the very end of their lives to learn how to live: and yet the larger portion of them leave this life confessing that they do not yet know how to live, and still less know how to live as wise men. Believe me, it requires a great man and one who is superior to human frailties not to allow any of his time to be filched from him: and therefore it follows that his life is a very long one, because he devotes every possible part of it to himself: no portion lies idle or uncultivated, or in another man's power; for he finds nothing worthy of being exchanged for his time, which he husbands most grudgingly.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: He had plenty of time. But those who gave most of their lives to serving the public never had enough. Don't think they weren't aware of what they were losing. You'll often hear these successful people cry out in the middle of their crowds of clients, their court cases, and all their prestigious troubles: "I'm not allowed to live my own life." Why not? Because everyone who asks for your help pulls you away from yourself. How many days have you lost to that defendant? That person running for office? That old woman tired of burying her heirs? That man faking illness to make his potential heirs greedy? That powerful friend who uses you as decoration in his entourage, not as a real friend?
original_excerpt: He, therefore, had time enough: whereas those who gave up a great part of their lives to the people of necessity had not enough. Yet you need not suppose that the latter were not sometimes conscious of their loss: indeed, you will hear most of those who are troubled with great prosperity every now and then cry out amid their hosts of clients, their pleadings in court, and their other honourable troubles, "I am not allowed to live my own life." Why is he not allowed? because all those who call upon you to defend them, take you away from yourself. How many of your days have been spent by that defendant? by that candidate for office? by that old woman who is weary with burying her heirs? by that man who pretends to be ill, in order to excite the greed of those who hope to inherit his property? by that powerful friend of yours, who uses you to swell his train, not to be his friend?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: Take stock of your life and look back at all your days. You'll see that only a few days — and only the ones that were useless for anything else — were truly yours.
original_excerpt: Balance your account, and run over all the days of your life; you will see that only a very few days, and only those which were useless for any other purpose, have been left to you.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: The politician who finally gets the power he craved now wants to get rid of it. He keeps asking, "When will this term be over?" Another man puts on expensive public games — something he once would have paid anything to do. Now he asks, "When can I escape from this?" There's the famous lawyer who packs the courthouse, drawing crowds that stretch beyond where they can even hear him speak. He asks, "When does vacation start?" Everyone rushes through life. They long for the future and grow tired of the present. But the person who uses all his time for his own purposes — who plans each day like he's planning his whole life — doesn't wish for tomorrow or fear it. What new pleasure could any hour bring him? He's experienced everything already, even to the point of being sick of it.
original_excerpt: He who has obtained the _fasces_[6] for which he longed, is eager to get rid of them, and is constantly saying, "When will this year be over?" another exhibits public games, and once would have given a great deal for the chance of doing so, but now "when," says he, "shall I escape from this?" another is an advocate who is fought for in all the courts, and who draws immense audiences, who crowd all the forum to a far greater distance than they can hear him; "When," says he, "will vacation-time come?" Every man hurries through his life, and suffers from a yearning for the future, and a weariness of the present: but he who disposes of all his time for his own purposes, who arranges all his days as though he were arranging the plan of his life, neither wishes for nor fears the morrow: for what new pleasure can any hour now bestow upon him? he knows it all, and has indulged in it all even to satiety.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7

plain_english: Fortune can do whatever she wants with everything else — this man's life is already safe from her. He might gain something, but he can't lose anything. He can only gain things the way someone who's already stuffed full might get some extra food that he takes even though he doesn't want it. So don't think someone has lived long just because he has wrinkles or gray hair. That man hasn't lived long — he's just been alive for a long time. Would you say a sailor had traveled far if a storm caught him right after leaving port and kept spinning him around in circles with winds blowing from every direction? That man hasn't sailed much. He's just been tossed around a lot.
original_excerpt: Fortune may deal with the rest as she will, his life is already safe from her: such a man may gain something, but cannot lose anything: and, indeed, he can only gain anything in the same way as one who is already glutted and filled can get some extra food which he takes although he does not want it. You have no grounds, therefore, for supposing that any one has lived long, because he has wrinkles or grey hairs: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive. Why! would you think that a man had voyaged much if a fierce gale had caught him as soon as he left his port, and he had been driven round and round the same place continually by a succession of winds blowing from opposite quarters? such a man has not travelled much, he has only been much tossed about.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 7
